content: In community settings, integrating HIV testing services with other health services, decentralizing these services to primary healthcare facilities and community locations, and sharing testing responsibilities with trained lay providers can enhance accessibility and uptake. Integration involves co-locating and sharing resources across various health areas, offering HIV testing, prevention, treatment, and care alongside services for tuberculosis (TB), viral hepatitis, sexually transmitted infections (STIs), maternal and child health, sexual and reproductive health, and harm-reduction programs for people who inject drugs. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends integrating HIV services, including testing, with these relevant clinical services to make testing more convenient and increase its uptake, particularly in high-prevalence settings. Integration should be tailored to the needs of specific populations and contexts. Decentralization of HIV testing services involves providing these services at peripheral health facilities, such as primary healthcare centers, and within communities. This approach can reduce transportation costs and waiting times, making testing more accessible, especially for men, young people, and key populations who may avoid facility-based testing. Collaboration between community programs and nearby health facilities can improve early enrollment in care. Decentralized sites should aim to provide rapid linkage to antiretroviral therapy (ART) and care services. However, decentralization may not always be suitable, as some individuals may prefer centralized services for greater anonymity, particularly in settings where stigma and discrimination are concerns. In low-prevalence settings, decentralization may also be inefficient and costly. Decisions on decentralization should consider the context, service gaps, and cost-effectiveness. Task sharing, a strategy endorsed by WHO, involves redistributing tasks from highly trained healthcare providers to those with shorter training, such as lay providers. This approach addresses shortages of trained health workers and increases the efficiency of the workforce. Trained lay providers can independently conduct safe and effective HIV testing using rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs). They can also provide pre-test information, perform tests, interpret results, report HIV status, offer post-test counseling, and support linkage to prevention, treatment, and care services. Peer workers can also be trained to function as lay providers. WHO recommends that trained and supervised lay providers deliver HIV testing services in both community and healthcare settings. A test-for-triage approach using single RDTs or HIV self-testing can further support community-based testing. For accurate HIV diagnosis, WHO advises using testing algorithms that achieve at least 99% positive predictive value, combining tests with high sensitivity and specificity. The first test in the algorithm should have the highest sensitivity, followed by tests with the highest specificity. Countries are encouraged to adopt a three-test strategy as HIV positivity rates fall below 5% in national programs. Dual HIV/syphilis RDTs can be used as the first test in antenatal care to increase testing and treatment coverage. Retesting before initiating ART is recommended to verify HIV status and minimize errors. However, retesting individuals already on ART is not advised, as it may yield incorrect results. For infants, early HIV testing and rapid initiation of treatment are critical due to high mortality rates among untreated HIV-positive infants. Virological testing using nucleic acid testing (NAT) is required to confirm HIV infection in infants, as maternal antibodies can persist up to 18 months. Testing at birth and at four to six weeks of age is recommended to identify infections early. Delays in obtaining results and linking infants to care remain challenges. Innovative approaches, such as point-of-care testing and birth NAT, can improve outcomes. However, birth testing should complement, not replace, testing at four to six weeks. Immediate ART initiation for infants with a positive test result is essential, even as confirmatory testing is conducted. In summary, integrating, decentralizing, and task-sharing HIV testing services, along with implementing accurate testing strategies and ensuring timely diagnosis and treatment, are critical components of effective HIV care. These approaches should be tailored to the needs of specific populations and settings to maximize their impact.
